name: Papaya extract

lead: Papaya extract is used in masks and cleansers as an enzyme exfoliant. People use it for smoother, brighter-looking skin.

Papaya latex contains papain, a protein-digesting enzyme that loosens dead surface cells, which is the basis for exfoliation. Papain is also used in meat tenderizers, wound debridement products and dental gels. No human trial of papaya extract for skin appearance was found; research covers other uses and animal studies.

paras: Used as a leave-on mask or rinse-off cleanser, typically once or a few times a week as a gentle alternative to acid exfoliants.
The FDA warned companies in 2008 to stop marketing topical papain drug products after hypersensitivity reports. People allergic to latex may also react to papaya.

angle.text: Papaya extract works as an enzyme exfoliant: papain digests protein in dead surface cells, leaving skin smoother and brighter. Trials of the extract for skin appearance were not found.

lead: Papaya extract is a preparation from the fruit, leaves, seeds or latex of Carica papaya. In skincare it is usually described as an enzyme exfoliant: papaya latex is the source of papain, a protein-digesting enzyme, and products use it to loosen dead surface cells so skin looks smoother and brighter.[1][2]

A second, separate use appears among lifters: papaya extract is sold as a digestive enzyme supplement, and T Nation members describe taking it to ease digestion of high-protein diets, which they connect to eating enough to build muscle.[3][4]

Papain is also used in meat tenderizers, enzymatic wound debridement products and dental caries gels.[1] No human trial of papaya extract for skin appearance was found; published research covers other uses, including a systematic review of papaya extract in dengue, and animal and in vitro studies.[5][6] In 2008 the US FDA warned companies to stop marketing topical papain drug products after reports of hypersensitivity reactions, and latex-allergic people may be at higher risk of reacting to papaya.[1]
infobox: Fruit/leaf extracts, enzyme exfoliants, digestive supplements
FDA 2008 warning on topical papain drug products[1]

paras: Carica papaya was first domesticated in Mesoamerica, in southern Mexico and Central America. The word papaya comes from Arawakan languages and entered English around 1600; Spaniards carried the plant to the Old World in the 16th century, and cultivation is now nearly pantropical.[2] Wikipedia notes that papain was used before European contact to tenderise meat in South America.[1]

All parts of the plant contain latex. Green fruit and latex are rich in papain, while skin, pulp and seeds hold carotenoids such as lutein, beta-carotene and lycopene, polyphenols and benzyl isothiocyanates.[2]

Papain (also called papaya proteinase I, EC 3.4.22.2) is a cysteine protease whose precursor has 345 amino acids; its active site is a Cys-25 and His-159 catalytic dyad, held by three disulfide bridges, and it works best at about 60 to 70 degrees C.[1] It is collected as latex from scored papaya fruit, dried and purified, and is used in leather, cosmetic, textile, detergent, food and pharmaceutical industries.[1]

Besides meat tenderiser powders, papain is an ingredient in wound-debridement preparations such as Accuzyme, which clear dead tissue from chronic wounds, and in the Papacarie caries-removal gel used in dentistry.[1] That protein-dissolving action on dead tissue is the basis for its use in exfoliating products.

Cosmetic products list papaya extract or papain as an enzymatic exfoliant, positioned as a milder alternative to acid peels because it targets proteins that bind surface cells together. The cited sources do not include a trial of this use for skin appearance.

T Nation members describe papaya extract as a supplement that eases digestion on high-protein diets, with several posts recommending it for gas after protein shakes.[3][4] A member recounts a supplement-store employee recommending it because it aids protein digestion.[7] These are personal reports.

A 2025 review of Carica papaya in health and disease describes traditional uses, nutrition, phytochemistry and pharmacology, reporting anti-inflammatory, wound-healing, antibacterial and other properties in laboratory and animal studies, and noting that toxicity, efficacy and clinical trials are needed before therapeutic use [8]. Fermented papaya preparations are a separate product type: registered trials include a skin barrier study in healthy volunteers (n=30, not yet recruiting), a study of systemic inflammation and aging (n=30), and a driving-simulator study in older adults (n=34) [9][10][11]. A 2019 review discusses papaya extract in cancer research [12], and a 2024 case report describes platelet recovery in a dengue patient treated with papaya leaf extract [13].

T Nation threads on digestive enzymes show lifters discussing whether enzymes are needed for protein digestion; one poster questioned why they would be, asking whether early humans evolved eating plenty of protein, while others recommended enzyme tablets to hard gainers trying to eat large amounts of food [14][15]. In a thread about protein farts a poster wrote that papaya extract 'gets rid of protein farts' [3]. These are anecdotes and opinions; no study cited here tests papaya extract in lifters.

No studies found for skin appearance. Related human evidence concerns other uses: a 2019 systematic review and meta-analysis examined papaya leaf extract in dengue fever.[5] Registered trials include a phase 3 randomised trial of Carica papaya in dengue (n=250),[16] a trial of topical papaya leaf extract 1% ointment versus mupirocin for limited impetigo (n=128),[17] and a study of carotenoid absorption from fresh papaya, tomato and carrot (n=16).[18] The registry records cited do not report results.

Other work is in animals, such as rat studies of leaf extract on blood glucose and 28-day toxicity,[6][19] and a polyurethane nanofiber burn dressing loaded with honey and papaya extract tested in vitro for hemocompatibility.[20]

On 23 September 2008 the FDA warned companies to stop marketing topical papain products, citing reports of hypersensitivity reactions with a serious fall in blood pressure and increased heart rate; affected products included Accuzyme, Panafil and Ziox. The agency advised concerned users to consult a healthcare provider.[1]

Unripe papaya releases latex that can irritate skin and cause allergic reactions, and papain can act as an allergen in sensitive people. Latex-allergic people may face a higher risk of reacting to papaya products.[1][2]
